title: How to find the 1 bad change in 1,000 with 10 tests
description:
When one of 1,000 changes broke your app, don't test them in order. Test the middle one: if it works, the bug came later; if it's broken, it came earlier. Either way half the suspects are gone, so 1,000 becomes 500, 250, 125, 63, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1: ten tests. A million changes takes 20 and a billion 30. Git does this for you with git bisect, which the Linux kernel docs use to find the change that broke a release.

Numbers checked in code: every possible bad change among 1,000 tested (worst case 10 tests), plus 100,000 random ones (average 9.98). Sources: git-scm.com, git-bisect documentation; docs.kernel.org, Bisecting a bug.

social_caption: One of 1,000 changes broke your app, and you can find it in 10 tests. Here's the halving trick behind git bisect.
facts_checked: git bisect 'uses a binary search algorithm to find which commit in your project's history introduced a bug': mark a bad and a good commit, it picks one between, you say good or bad, until it finds the exact commit; its own example prints '675 revisions left to test after this (roughly 10 steps)' (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-bisect)
Linux kernel docs: how to use git bisect 'to find the source code change that broke something', e.g. after upgrading from Linux 6.0 to 6.1 (https://docs.kernel.org/admin-guide/bug-bisect.html)
1,000 changes: worst case 10 tests over all 1,000 possible bad changes; 100,000 random ones: 9 to 10 tests, mean 9.98 (verify.py)
A million changes: 20 tests; a billion: 30 (ceil log2; verify.py)

beats.say: Your app broke. Check 1,000 changes, or just 10?
Not a smarter debugger, and not luck. You just stop checking in order.
Last week it worked. Since then, your team made 1,000 changes, and one of them broke the login.
Jump to change 500 and test it. It works? Then the bug came later. 500 suspects gone in one test.
Jump to 750. Broken? Now it's between 500 and 750.
Every test cuts the pile in half, whatever the answer. So how many cuts from 1,000 down to 1?
And it barely grows. A million changes? 20 tests. A billion? 30.
Git does it for you. Git bisect picks the middle every time, and Linux developers use it to find the change that broke a release.
